source.title: Ensuring medical AI safety: interpretability-driven detection and mitigation of spurious model behavior and associated data
source.authors: Frederik Pahde; Thomas Wiegand; S. Lapuschkin; W. Samek

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses individual neurons as candidate bias representations and reports their artifact-retrieval performance, but it does not test the claim's estimates about how many neuron poles have one or more understandable jobs.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses neuron redundancy and polysemanticity, and compares individual-neuron bias scores with CAV scores for retrieving medical-artifact samples. Those retrieval results do not measure the share of neuron poles with a single understandable job, explanation fidelity on held-out activations, or the other claim versions. The rows below record one explicit retrieval comparison as a related finding, not as a test of a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper is a medical shortcut-detection and mitigation framework. It uses single neurons and CAVs as bias representations and reports only its own pipeline's retrieval, localization and mitigation performance. It never estimates the share of neurons with one understandable job. It does not score neuron explanations on held-out activations, revisit InceptionV1 polysemantic examples, or build neuron-level attribution graphs. Its mentions of polysemanticity and superposition are citations of prior work, not results.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that their extended Reveal2Revise framework can semi-automatically detect, annotate, localize and mitigate spurious artifacts across four medical datasets with VGG16, ResNet50 and ViT. They report that CAVs generally beat single neurons for sample retrieval and that layer choice is crucial. They frame neuron redundancy and polysemanticity as limitations taken from prior work, not as their own findings.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses neuron- and CAV-based bias representations for medical-artifact retrieval and mitigation; it does not perform the pole-level interpretability audit or held-out explanation tests described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that retrieval performance depends on layer and artifact type; for example, layers closer to the model head detect pacemaker samples while earlier layers fail.

fits_no_version.finding: Across layers and artifacts, the best single neuron (selected on validation) generally ranks artifact samples worse than an SVM-CAV. For example, ResNet50 Block 3 microscope reaches AP 0.26 for the neuron versus 0.86 for the CAV (AUROC 0.76 vs 0.98). Some neurons match CAVs, e.g. timestamp AP 0.83 for both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For retrieving samples with labeled spurious artifacts in medical CNNs, a single best neuron is usually a weaker concept detector than a linear direction (CAV), with the gap depending on artifact and layer.

record.problems: The reported neuron results concern retrieval of labeled medical artifacts, not semantic interpretability or the claimed pole-level job shares. The paper states that layer choice matters and that its framework requires human supervision.
record.rows_left_out: Other neuron-versus-CAV retrieval results across layers, artifacts, and model architectures appear in Appendix A.7.2, Tables 5 and 6. They are not extracted here because the retrieval measure does not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: All: no pole-level job-share audit of Qwen3-32B or any LLM.
All: no interpretable-neuron shares across language models or scales; only CNN and ViT medical classifiers are studied.
All: no InceptionV1 cat/car analysis and no test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
All: no measured share of interpretable neurons by architecture or tooling. Remarks that ViT last-layer neurons are hard to interpret are qualitative only.
All: no neuron-based attribution graphs, and no comparison against replacement models.
All: no test of whether activating-example explanations predict firing on new inputs.
All: no simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: These are retrieval comparisons inside the study's own method, not tests of the claim, so arguably they should not be rows at all. Neuron interpretability is discussed only qualitatively, e.g. 'hard-to-interpret concepts (neurons) #89 and #143'. No neuron-share measurements appear anywhere.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole-level job-share estimates and whether neuron poles generally have one main job.
Interpretable-neuron shares across model families, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain interpretability rates or the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a replacement model.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples predict where a neuron fires on new activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Rank unseen samples for the microscope artifact using a single-neuron bias score.
rows.note: The tables compare CAV and single-neuron retrieval scores. This measures artifact retrieval, not how many neuron poles have one understandable job.
rows.check: Values check out: Table 5 gives CAV AP 0.86 and Table 6 gives best-neuron AP 0.26 (ResNet50 Block 3, microscope). This is a retrieval comparison inside the study's own method, not a measure of any version. The best neuron was selected on the validation set, and the row is a comparator, not evidence on the claim.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Rank unseen samples for the microscope artifact using a single-neuron bias score.
rows.note: This retrieval comparison does not evaluate semantic job count or explanation fidelity.
rows.check: Baseline is misread. In Table 5, ResNet50 Block 3 microscope CAV AUROC is 0.98, not 0.92 (0.92 is the ruler AP column). The neuron AUROC of 0.76 is correct. The row is a comparison inside the study's own method and bears on no version.
